pattern: A step concludes a named thing is ABSENT after consulting one of the several views a distribution ships for that class of thing, and reports the conclusion as a fact about the distribution rather than as a fact about what it read. The disclosure is not what is missing -- such a step routinely names the files it opened and the zero it found in them -- so a reader auditing the artefact sees a complete, honest, wrong answer. What is missing is the comparison between the views that exist and the views that were opened.
docstring: A refusal that a declared name is ABSENT must be falsified against the views the step did not read -- and the falsification must ask through the DECLARATION GRAMMAR for that class of thing, never through a free-text search. It fires only when the refused name is actually DECLARED in a view the step did not open. The step already owns a parser for that grammar, so the check reuses it rather than inventing a search.
fix_action: On any verdict asserting a declared name is absent, take the name from the step's own artefact, enumerate the view directories of the resolved tree, subtract the ones the artefact says were read, and run the step's OWN declaration parser over the remainder. A declared hit means the refusal is false and names the file. No hit means the refusal stands and the check is silent.
measured_red_green: Both arms, with the negative control: PDK declares the name in the unread view -> FIRES, naming the file it is findable in. PDK declares it nowhere -> silent, and a genuine absence stays a genuine absence. `_jcapsha_notes/evidence/f1_final_probe.py`.
supersedes: An earlier version of this record proposed pinning the INPUT SET of a re-implementation against its upstream, caught by a set difference. That rule is REFUTED and the refutation is measured, not argued -- see `_jcapsha_notes/evidence/f1_input_set_pin_REFUTED.txt`. Over its whole population of 5 modules it over-fires (43 findings under the natural scoping, 4 of 5 modules), and under every narrowing that reduces the over-firing it stops catching the defect it was written for: the control on the pre-fix tree reports an empty unaccounted list. The reason is structural -- the dropped variable is declared in the upstream PDK variable table and consumed in a shared helper, and is not a member of the upstream step's own declared inputs, so no set difference over that step's contract can contain it.
why_the_disclosure_form_is_not_the_rule: The finding was first generalised as 'a step that cannot find a declared thing must say WHICH views it read'. Driving the pre-fix producer, the refusal record already enumerated the exact file it read, the zero records found in it, and the empty result -- so a guard written to that rule runs clean on the buggy tree. The rule with teeth is not about naming what was read, it is about comparing it to what exists.
prior_art_checked: programs/gate_discloses_denominator_check.py, programs/_gate_denominator.py, programs/gate_zero_denominator_refuses_check.py, programs/_sweep_reach.py, programs/_shape_refusal.py -- five programs already own the DISCLOSURE half, and all five pass the pre-fix refusal, because the pre-fix refusal discloses. None of them compares what was read against what the distribution ships. No existing program makes that comparison.
formulation_history: THIRD formulation; the first two were swept and dropped, and one of them was adopted before it was swept, which is the mistake worth recording. (1) pin the input SET against upstream -- over-fires 4 of 5 and, once narrowed by upstream's own pdk flag, stops catching the defect at all. (2) a refusal must have READ every view -- fires on the defect, but sweeping it afterwards found 8 of the 10 in-scope programs read exactly one view for good reasons, so it is the same bug from the other side. Full sequence: `_jcapsha_notes/evidence/f1_three_formulations.txt`.
false_positive_sweep: MEASURED on both real open PDKs in the pinned image, and it REFUTED the version I had published. The bare substring form over-fires: a short generic name hits an unrelated node-info file on both PDKs, and a plausible-but-absent name hits a circuit-simulator init file on one and a device-model file on the other. My claim that it was silent 'by construction' was an argument, not a measurement, and it was wrong. Asking the same question through the declaration grammar is clean on all four probes on both PDKs: the genuinely declared site fires with its size; the nonexistent name, the short generic name and the plausible-but-absent name are all silent. `_jcapsha_notes/evidence/f1_formulation3_fp_MEASURED.txt`.
measured_population: ONE, and this is the seventh correction to my own claims in this capture. The amended rule says the falsification must use the step's OWN declaration parser, so it applies only where such a parser exists. Of the 10 in-scope modules -- those that refuse on a named absence after a lookup into a distribution view -- exactly ONE owns a declaration parser. After four formulations, a red/green pair and a clean false-positive profile on two real distributions, F1 is a correct and well-measured SINGLE-SITE rule, not the general one I kept presenting it as.
the_widening_i_did_not_take: There is a stronger reading: rather than 'use the parser you have', demand that ANY step refusing on absence OWN a parser for the declaration grammar of the thing it refuses about. Under that reading the population is 10 and the rule fires on 9. I did NOT adopt it, and the reason is the whole history of this record: 9-of-10 is the exact shape that has been wrong six times in this capture, and I have not measured whether those 9 refuse about things that HAVE a declaration grammar at all -- several refuse about our own artefacts, which have none. The widening is named here so it is not lost, and flagged as UNSWEPT so nobody adopts it the way I adopted formulation 2.

pattern: A step re-implements an upstream computation and its arithmetic drifts from upstream's, in a direction no test covers because both agree on the inputs the tests use. The drift surfaces later as an unrelated refusal rather than as a wrong number, so it is attributed to the thing that refused instead of to the arithmetic. Here the along-the-row extent was taken from the ORIENTED footprint while upstream takes the master's width in both places it measures, on all four sides.
docstring: A re-implementation must DECLARE which upstream computation it mirrors and which primitive that computation measures with; the declaration is then checkable, and the check is a program. Detection without the declaration is NOT a program -- see the generality sweep -- so the deterministic work is the declaration format plus the checker that reads the named upstream file, confirms the named primitive is what it uses, and asserts our function does not transform it before aggregating.
fix_action: Walk the placement function's assignments and taint every name whose value flows from the orientation-dependent footprint helper. Refuse if the along-the-row extent is tainted. The upstream source that fixes the expected primitive is read from the pinned image at run time, not quoted from memory, and the gate returns NOT DETERMINED rather than PASS when it cannot read it.
measured_red_green: The one-computation pin, both arms: RED on origin/main (16 orientation-tainted names, the along-the-row extent among them), GREEN on the fix branch (2, both corner extents). `_jcapsha_notes/evidence/f2_pin_probe.py`. That measurement stands; what it does NOT establish, and what my earlier version of this record wrongly claimed it did, is that the same predicate generalises.
upstream_confirmed_by_reading: The upstream side-arithmetic loop computes both a width and a height per instance and sums ONLY the width, in a loop that is side-agnostic. Read out of the pinned image on 2026-08-22, not cited from the source report.
prior_art_checked: VERIFIED over program bodies, not names: 6 programs both reference an upstream tree and use comparison language; reading all six, NONE pins one of our computations against upstream's. They cite upstream as documentation for what to expect -- the good habit -- and compare things within our own artefacts. `sta_engine_parity_check` pins two SHIPPED BINARIES against each other at run time; `_electrical_mention` and `_submission_template` stop two of OUR OWN halves drifting; `size_policy_drift_check` reconciles five of our own mechanisms; `ip_catalog_upstream_audit` pins vendored FILE COPIES by hash. No existing program makes an upstream computation's primitive executable against ours. Evidence: `_jcapsha_notes/evidence/prior_art_claims_VERIFIED.txt`.
why_a_cited_upstream_is_not_enough: MEASURED on the pre-fix tree: the correct upstream rule was written down ONE LINE ABOVE the code that violates it. The comment says the upstream primitive is used on every side; the next statement takes the orientation-dependent extent. The knowledge was present, correct, and cited -- it was simply not executable, and nothing compared the prose to the code. That is the whole case for this rule: the repo already has the discipline of reading upstream rather than remembering it, and several modules say so in those words, but the reading freezes into a comment at authoring time and is never re-checked against the code beneath it.
generality_sweep: MEASURED, and it refutes the generality my earlier version of this record claimed. The taint-walk predicate I measured red/green is written for ONE computation. Swept over the population -- the modules that cite an upstream computation by path -- the SHAPE it keys on (a value flowing through a transform into an aggregate) occurs at 224 sites. That shape is just what ordinary code looks like. A program cannot pick the one site of 224 that matters.
the_exact_decision_it_cannot_make: Named as the ladder requires, rather than waved at. INPUT the program would see: the AST of our module and the text of the upstream file. DECISION it cannot make from that input: the CORRESPONDENCE -- which of our functions re-implements which upstream loop. Neither text declares it. Our function does not say which upstream loop it mirrors, and the upstream loop does not say what re-implements it. BUT THAT MISSING INPUT IS DECLARABLE, not unknowable, which is why this stays Bucket A rather than becoming a judgement call: the information already exists in the module as PROSE -- it cites the upstream file by path, and on the pre-fix tree the comment one line above the defect names the correct primitive. Turning that prose into a declaration is a one-line change per site and converts an undecidable detection into a decidable check.

title: The IO-row builder applies its two named rotation arguments to each other's rows
problem: The IO-row builder takes one rotation argument named for the horizontal rows and one named for the vertical rows. MEASURED across seven separate tool processes, one per argument pair so no row from an earlier pass could be reused by a later one: varying the HORIZONTAL argument moves the WEST and EAST pads and leaves the SOUTH and NORTH pads untouched, and varying the VERTICAL argument moves the SOUTH and NORTH pads and leaves WEST and EAST untouched. Row identity was confirmed by die position, not by trusting the row names: the pad on the west row sits at the offset from the low-X edge and the pad on the south row at the offset from the low-Y edge. The tool's own script layer is CORRECT: dumping the command body from the running binary shows the two arguments bound to their own variables and passed to the row builder in the documented order, so the crossing is below the script layer, in the compiled row builder. Reproduced on two builds about 440 commits apart.
tool_enhancement: In the compiled IO-row builder that the script layer calls with (horizontal rotation, vertical rotation, corner rotation, ring index), the horizontal rotation must be applied to the rows that run horizontally and the vertical rotation to the rows that run vertically. They are currently exchanged. The fix belongs in the fork of this tool: a plugin-side rule could only paper over it, because the plugin does not place the rows and any correction it applied would be a second guess layered on the first.
pattern: A tool exposes two named arguments that select between two symmetric cases, and applies each to the other's case. The symmetry is what hides it: at the default, where both arguments carry the same value, the two wrong assignments are indistinguishable from the two right ones, so nothing fires until someone sets exactly one of them. A caller who sets the one named for the case they care about sees no change and concludes the argument is INERT, which is a different and much less alarming defect than the one they have.
suggested_fix: Exchange the two parameters at the point the compiled row builder consumes them, and pin the fix with the two-arm measurement in the bad sample: hold one argument at the default and vary the other, in separate processes, asserting that only the rows the varied argument NAMES move. A single-arm probe cannot tell an inert argument from a crossed one, which is how this was first recorded as inertness.
session_context: Found while capturing a pad-ring recovery. The source report recorded the horizontal-side pad tracking the vertical argument as a SEPARATE oddity, observed and not chased. Running the decisive second arm turned it into the whole explanation.
why_bucket_t: The root cause is inside a forked tool this flow drives. The plugin cannot fix it: it does not build the rows. Anything the plugin did here would be a correction applied on top of a wrong one, which is the definition of papering over.
component_note: The honest home for a forked-tool record is the STEP it surfaced in, but `backlog_sanitize_check.COMPONENT_RE` cannot express any step id -- see the `component_vocabulary_admits_its_namespace` record in this same batch. `program:pad_ring_gen` is the program whose verdict the tool defect blocks, and the `generating_step` field above already carries the step. The regex was NOT widened to make this record fit: widening a regex to turn a red green is forbidden, and it is forbidden most exactly when the red is mine.

pattern: A step accepts a config variable the tool underneath does not honour as named, and proceeds without saying so. The author who set it is told nothing, and the artefact records a value that did not reach the geometry. The mirrored failure is a step that discloses the defect for the ONE variable it happened to measure and leaves the sibling variable, which is the one the tool actually mis-applies, unguarded.
docstring: The degradation contract for a config variable a step accepts but cannot honour. At the value indistinguishable from never having set it: PROCEED, and carry the non-honouring record, with its measurement, in EVERY report the step emits INCLUDING its skips, because a disclosure present only on the happy path is not a disclosure. At any deliberately declared other value: exit 2 NOT DETERMINED naming the variable, never 0 and never 1, because being unable to honour a request is neither a pass nor a finding about the design. The rule is the contract, not the one variable: every variable the same tool call carries is in scope, not only the one that was measured.
fix_action: Require, for any step that declares a variable unhonoured: the non-honouring record is a key of the BASE report template rather than of one branch, so it survives every early return; a deliberately declared value exits 2; and the guarded set covers every variable passed in the same tool call as the measured one. Drive the step's skip path and its proceed path and require the key in both, and drive it with a declared value and require exit 2.
why_this_rule_and_not_the_one_variable: The ruling that produced this was written for one variable. MEASURED here, the sibling variable is the one that silently changes the geometry the ruling was protecting, and the shipped guard does not cover it, so a run that declares the sibling and leaves the measured one alone passes the guard and gets an artefact whose recorded orientation contradicts the tool. Generalising the rule to the tool CALL rather than the variable closes that.
prior_art_checked: `adder_map_techmap.py` states the general rule in prose in its own header and enforces it for its ONE knob, by requiring evidence from the tool's own log. Three other modules state a version of it for their own case. No module inherits it, and no program checks it. `waiver_staleness.py` refuses a waiver whose reason no longer holds, and `dead_timing_constant_warn.py` finds declared constants nothing references; neither asks whether a declared input REACHED the tool.
measured_population: FOUR independent instances on the current tree, in four different subsystems, found by sweeping 1232 programs for a not-honoured claim whose subject is a NAMED TOOL rather than one of our own gates: a declared synthesis techmap that silently does not bind; a delay target the mapper silently ignores; a declared placement construct the layout stream-out does not honour, in two programs; and this one. Of the four, ZERO carry the non-honouring as a machine-readable record -- all four wrote the lesson as prose in whichever module happened to find it. That is the argument for making it a contract: the repo has now discovered this class four times and absorbed it zero times.
failure_signature: Measured across the instances, the class has one signature: the artefact is INDISTINGUISHABLE from never having set the input. One instance produced a byte-identical netlist, and cost 22 percent of a timing path before anyone looked; this one produces an identical ring at the default because the two arguments that are crossed carry the same value there. That is why the class survives review -- there is nothing in the output to review.
landing_status: Correct but RED on the current tree, and the red is 4 true positives rather than a false one: none of the four instances meets either half of the contract. This supersedes an earlier claim in this batch that the rule had no population and was premature to land -- that claim was made without measuring and it was wrong. The population is the work list for whoever lands it.

design: (found while capturing, not one of the three findings)
pattern: A validator advertises an accepted vocabulary of the form PREFIX:IDENTIFIER, one prefix per namespace, and its character class cannot express the identifiers of one of those namespaces. The advertised form is then unusable for every member of that namespace, and the failure is invisible from the validator's side: it reports a well-formed refusal naming the very form the author used, so the author reads it as their own mistake and substitutes a different prefix. Nobody files it, because each individual author works around it in one line.
docstring: Every prefix a component-vocabulary validator advertises must accept the identifiers of the namespace that prefix names. Deterministic form: for each advertised prefix, enumerate the namespace it points at from that namespace's own source of truth, and require the validator to accept every member. A prefix whose namespace is empty or unenumerable is refused as unverifiable rather than assumed fine.
fix_action: Enumerate each namespace from its declared source and assert the validator accepts every member, as a test that fails when either the regex or the namespace changes. Do NOT simply widen the character class in isolation: the test is what keeps the two in step, and the widening without it would drift again the next time a namespace gains a character.
measured: The advertised form for the step namespace admits 0 of the 39 step ids in the capture routing table, and 6 of the 69 ids in the canonical flow are inexpressible -- every one of the six a dotted inserted step, one of which is the step this whole capture is about. No shipped record in the backlog corpus uses that prefix, which is what an unusable form looks like from the outside: not an error, an absence.
why_not_fixed_here: The fix would widen a regex, and it would do so on the exact night that regex refused a record of mine. The standing rule is that a red is never made to go away by relaxing what asks the question, and it binds hardest when the red is my own. Captured, measured, and left red.
prior_art_checked: No program compares an accepted-vocabulary regex against the namespace it names. `programs/p0_gate_invocability_drift_check.py` is the nearest neighbour -- it pins the gates a registry declares but cannot invoke -- and it is about argv, not about an identifier grammar.
measured_population: ONE. Swept for validators carrying a PREFIX:IDENTIFIER alternation: exactly one in 1232 programs. This is a real defect with a real measurement, but it is a SINGLE INSTANCE, not a class with a corpus, and it is recorded as such rather than dressed as a general rule. `_jcapsha_notes/evidence/f4_population_MEASURED.txt`.
